historical_location: North Carolina coastal plain (lower Neuse River), between Neuse River and Contentnea Creek
documentation_source: John Lawson's word list (1709), containing 143 attested words

historical_context.tribe_information: Woccon tribe first documented in 1701 by John Lawson
historical_context.location: About two leagues east of the southern villages of the Tuscarora tribe, near present-day Goldsboro/Snow Hill (Wayne/Greene County)
historical_context.fate: Last mentioned in 1712 treaty; likely absorbed by Tuscarora following the Tuscarora wars of 1711-1713

consonantal_phonemes.note: defective in Catawba, cannot occur word-initially

phonological_processes.description: In some words, a long oral vowel in Catawba corresponds to a nasal vowel in Woccon
Instances of m and n before oral vowels became p and d in Catawba but not in Woccon
Voicing of p and t before voiced consonants

Woccon_to_Catawba.note: In Catawba, m often became p before oral vowels
In Catawba, n often became d before oral vowels
In Catawba, initial r appears as d before oral vowels and n before nasal vowels

simple_words.description: Words composed of a single morpheme

complex_words.description: Words composed of two or more morphemes

reduplication.description: Repetition of all or part of a root to signal frequency or intensity

examples.derivation: From root kit- (break in two) with reduplication
From root pẽ:ʔ (step) with frequentive reduplication

number_system.description: Numbers show internal structure with identifiable roots

numerals.note: transcription error in original; likely 'Tonne hauk sea'

number_system.note: Possible subtractive formation for 7 and 8 meaning '(10) lacking 3' and '(10) lacking 2'

suffixes.function: indicates natural phenomena or repeated actions
nominal suffix, often in terms for animate beings

modes.name: participial
modes.description: Used as ending on verbs in compound verbal construction or as nominalizer

possession.description: Inalienably possessed nouns mark possessor with prefix; alienably possessed nouns mark possessor with suffix

examples.possessive_gloss: leggings with third person possessive suffix

pronominal_marking.description: Pronominal objects marked by proclitics, with third person singular objects unmarked

numeral_patterns.name: teens
numeral_patterns.description: Add -pea after the base number (ten + X)

numeral_patterns.name: multiples of ten
numeral_patterns.description: Use compound forms combining napnẽ: (ten) with the multiplier

relic_forms.note: This appears to be a relic form in Catawba, where the usual root for fire is [ipi?]
This appears to be a relic form in Catawba, a compound of [yana] tree and [pis] skin

word_order.head_modifier: Head noun followed by modifier (Object-Verb syntax)
word_order.note: Limited syntactic information available due to nature of word list documentation

relation_to_catawba.classification: Part of Coastal Catawban language family
relation_to_catawba.dialectal_features: Woccon maintained certain archaic features not preserved in Catawba
relation_to_catawba.note: Woccon was spoken on the eastern edge of the territory while Catawba was spoken at the southwestern edge

dialects.relation_to_catawba_simple: Distant relative in Eastern Siouan subfamily
dialects.note: Woccon and Catawba show considerable divergence despite genetic relationship

community_grammar_notes.text: It seems that dápa may have meant (wild) animal in Proto-Catawban, a meaning retained in Woccon but only in compounds in Catawba
community_grammar_notes.source_excerpt:
Raw-skin [wild animal] *dápa: W (Teep) 'Raw-skin undrest' C dápa 'something, some', dapadá·re· ‘he hunts (compare dáre· ‘he goes'), dapa- "prefix on animal names". (It seems that dápa may have meant (wild) animal in Proto-Catawban, a meaning retained in Woccon but only in compounds in Catawba.) of animals, names for some manufactured items, and at least one verb. The "root" appears to be cognate with
the independent word dápa some, something' Examples in- clude dapahí ye 'alligator (dapa + yehiye
water'), dapamá-ya? 'boat, watercraft' (compare namá-ya? 'boat, canoe, dugout, pirogue'), and
dapadá-?hire- 'he hunts' (compare dá·?hire· 'he goes'). Although there is no cognate for the stem
building root |dapa- in Woccon, the same process appears to be at work with a different morpheme.
